summaries.summary: Political tweet NLP may aid election nowcasting, forecasting, and issue identification, while BIBREF2 found crowdworkers matched experts accurately and budget-efficiently for sentiment labels.
The paper asks how accurately existing NLP tools answer "What sentiment?" and "Towards whom?" for BIBREF2's political tweets dataset.
Experiments reveal entity-level sentiment analysis is difficult for existing tools, while recognition of the entity, here which politician, was easier.

NLP toolkits typically provide tokenization, PoS tagging, chunking, named entity recognition, and sentiment analysis, with NER approaches including rule-based, statistical, and recurrent neural networks with attention modules.

SentiStrength and TensiStrength are rule-based sentiment tools using dictionaries and rules, with TensiStrength reporting sentiment towards selected entities based on five relaxation and five stress levels.

The authors selected BIBREF17 and BIBREF18 as publicly accessible commercial APIs for domain-agnostic entity-level sentiment analysis and also report results for TensiStrength, TwitterNLP, BIBREF19, CogComp-NLP, and Stanford NLP NER.
The 1,000-tweet dataset by BIBREF2 contains named-entities labels and entity-level sentiments for Bernie Sanders, Donald Trump, Hillary Clinton, and Ted Cruz from US crowdworkers and experts.
BIBREF2's decision tree assigns 2, 3, 5, or 7 workers based on tweet length, links, sarcasm signals, and disagreement, with sarcastic tweets allocated more crowdworkers.
Two experiment sets used BIBREF23, BIBREF17, and BIBREF18 for entity-level sentiment analysis, and BIBREF17, BIBREF19, BIBREF24, BIBREF25, BIBREF26, and BIBREF18 for named-entity recognition.
TwitterNLP used default values, Stanford NER used the 3-class model, CogComp-NLP NER used Ontonotes 5.0 NER model BIBREF27, and spaCy NER used the `en_core_web_lg' model.

Results use correct classification rate (CCR), defined for sentiment analysis as correctly-predicted sentiments over groundtruth sentiments and for NER as correctly predicted entities over groundtruth entities.
The 1,000 randomly selected tweets contain more than twice as many tweets about Trump, with crowdworker NER CCR at 98.6% and automated systems ranging from 77.2% to 96.7%.

Groundtruth labels contain 210 positive, 521 neutral, and 305 negative sentiments, with CCR of 31.7% for Rosette Text Analytics, 43.2% for Google Cloud, 44.2% for TensiStrength, and 74.7% for crowdworkers.
Crowdworkers correctly identified 62% neutral, 85% positive, and 92% negative sentiments, while Google Cloud, TensiStrength, and Rosette Text Analytics showed varied class-specific CCRs.

Existing NLP systems cannot accurately perform sentiment analysis of political tweets in the dataset, so future work will train a balanced crowdworker-labeled machine-learning NLP system using state-of-the-art deep neural networks.

The authors acknowledge support from the Hariri Institute for Computing and Computational Science & Engineering at Boston University and a Google Faculty Research Award, plus help from Daniel Khashabi, Mike Thelwal, and the Stanford NLP group.
